title: Write For The Readers You Can’t See
author: Rich Carr
summary: Carr, writing as a learning scientist, explains why a writer's visible engagement numbers badly understate the trust being built with silent readers. He starts from a short Note of his that resonated widely and asks why its closing line, write for the readers you can't see, landed. His answer draws on three bodies of research: the lurker ratio in online communities, Robert Zajonc's mere exposure effect with its inverted-U curve, and predictive processing, in which relevant surprise triggers a dopamine teaching signal. Working memory limits of three to five chunks, following Nelson Cowan, explain why a compact Note can outlast a sprawling essay. From this he derives a practical stance: be predictable, consistent and kind so that repeated low-friction exposure turns an idea into familiar furniture. He ends with three rules, hold one thought, make the surprise relevant and stay put, and a reminder that the unseen readers are the reason the work exists.
points: Carr cites the finding that thirteen to fifteen people read for every one who likes or comments, so a post with three likes may have reached fifty readers.
Mere exposure research suggests trust grows through repeated, low-friction contact, though pure repetition without variation bends the curve back down.
He distinguishes random surprise, which confuses, from relevant surprise, which forces the brain to update its model and pay attention.
Working memory limits mean one observation, one mechanism and one instruction can fit in a reader's head where a long essay often cannot.
His closing advice is to hold one thought, resolve any surprise quickly, and stay consistent long enough for exposure to build trust.
quotes: Someone can take that piece in and never tap a heart. They read it in a parked car. They read it again on Sunday night. They are still taking it in.
For every person who likes or comments, thirteen to fifteen read and never mark the post. The post that “got three likes” was sitting with fifty people. They just didn’t tell you.
You do not have to argue someone into trust. Repeated, low-friction contact with the same stimulus is enough for the brain to treat it as safer than the unfamiliar alternative.
Because nice is a costume. Kind is a stance. Nice hopes you like the post. Kind is willing to be useful even if the like never comes.
Random surprise creates confusion. Relevant surprise creates a moment where the brain has to look.
A long essay that tries to be a book chapter often does not fit within those limits. The silent reader can keep a Note. They cannot keep your archive.
Silence, in that frame, is not absence. It is reduced cognitive tax…the bill the brain stops sending you for having to figure out who this person is this time.
